name: Ghodaghodi Tal
tagline: A Ramsar lake chain beside the highway, full of birds and crocodiles
meta_description: Ghodaghodi Tal guide: Ramsar-listed lakes in Kailali with birds, mugger crocodiles and turtles, a lakeside temple and Tharu villages on the way west.
summary: Ghodaghodi Tal is a chain of forest lakes in Kailali district, listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2003 and declared a bird sanctuary in 2022. It lies right beside the East-West Highway near Sukhad, so it makes an easy two-to-three-hour stop between Bardia and Shuklaphanta.
intro: Most people drive past Ghodaghodi Tal without knowing it. The East-West Highway runs along its southern shore near Sukhad bazaar, and from a bus window you see only a flash of water and lotus leaves through the trees. Stop, walk ten minutes into the forest, and you are in one of the richest wetlands in the western Terai. Buses and trucks roar past a few hundred metres away, yet herons stand motionless in the shallows and crocodiles bask on the far banks.

Ghodaghodi is not one lake but a cluster of oxbow lakes and marshes at the foot of the Siwalik hills, linked by streams and surrounded by sal and riverine forest. The protected Ramsar site covers about 2,563 hectares at around 205 m. The main lake is the largest, with smaller lakes scattered through the forest around it. Water levels rise and fall with the seasons, and in winter wide margins of mud and reed attract waders and ducks.

For travellers the appeal is birds and reptiles at close range, with almost no other visitors. A survey in February 2021 counted 26 mugger crocodiles across 18 lakes, and the red-crowned roofed turtle, one of Asia's rarest freshwater turtles, lives here. In winter the open water fills with ducks, and herons and kingfishers work the edges year-round. Because it lies on the main road, it costs very little time to see.

story.title: A forest wetland on the old Terai trail
paras: Before the East-West Highway reached this part of the Terai in the late 20th century, the forest of Kailali was a thinly settled land of Tharu villages, malaria and wildlife. The lakes of Ghodaghodi were fishing grounds and places of worship for the Tharu, who still keep shrines in the forest and on the shore. When the road came it brought settlers from the hills, timber traffic and new pressure on the forest and water, and the bazaar of Sukhad grew up beside the lakes.

In August 2003 Ghodaghodi Tal was listed under the Ramsar Convention as a wetland of international importance. The listing recognised its value for rare reptiles and waterbirds, and as a stepping stone in the forest corridor that links the Siwalik hills to the plains, used by wildlife moving across the far western Terai. It was a significant step for a wetland outside any national park, managed largely with local communities. For local people the listing brought new attention and, with it, new responsibilities for the forest and water.

In March 2022 the area was declared a bird sanctuary, and local community forest groups now share in its care. Pressures remain: fishing, grazing, invasive plants and the highway itself. But the lakes are a good example of how a small, community-managed wetland can still hold crocodiles, otters and rare turtles within sight of a busy road. A quiet walk along the shore shows both sides: the beauty of the lakes and the marks of human use around them. Visiting with a local guide and paying any community fee helps keep that balance in favour of the wetland.

people: The villages around the lakes are mostly Tharu, joined since the 1960s by Chhetri, Brahmin and Dalit families from the hills of Doti, Achham and Bajura. In the 2011 census about 41 percent of Ghodaghodi municipality spoke Tharu at home, with Nepali, Doteli and Achhami the other main languages. Families farm rice and wheat, fish in the lakes and run shops and eateries in Sukhad bazaar on the highway.

Ghodaghodi Tal was declared a bird sanctuary in March 2022, adding protection for the waterbirds that winter on the lakes. It also protects the wetland's role as a resting place for migrating ducks and waders.

local_words.meaning: Lotus, growing on the lake edges

taste.name: Machha bhat
taste.text: Freshwater fish curry with rice, the everyday meal of the western Terai. The fish is cooked in mustard oil with turmeric, chilli and tomato and served with rice, lentils and a pickle. Eat it at one of the eating houses in Sukhad bazaar on the highway after your lake walk.

Ramsar wetland, mugger crocodiles, winter waterbirds

highlights.title: Lakeshore forest walk
highlights.text: A path leads from the highway into the forest around the main lake, with views across open water, lotus beds and reed edges. In two or three hours you can walk part of the shore, stopping at viewpoints for birds and basking crocodiles.

highlights.title: Winter waterbirds
highlights.text: From November to March ducks, grebes, cormorants and herons gather on the open water, with kingfishers, jacanas and purple swamphens along the margins. The bird sanctuary status since 2022 has made the lakes a quiet stop for birders driving west.

highlights.title: Mugger crocodiles
highlights.text: Ghodaghodi's lakes hold a healthy population of mugger crocodiles, the broad-snouted marsh crocodile of South Asia. On sunny winter days they haul out on the banks; scan the far shores with binoculars from the forest path.

highlights.title: The lakeside temple
highlights.text: A small Hindu temple stands near the main lake, where local people of every community come to offer flowers and light lamps, especially at festivals. It is a calm place to watch village life by the water.

highlights.title: An easy stop on the highway
highlights.text: Because the lakes lie just off the East-West Highway near Sukhad, they fit easily into the drive between Bardia and Shuklaphanta, breaking a long day with a walk, birds and a meal. A two-hour stop is enough to see the best of the lakes.

how_to_reach.text: Ghodaghodi Tal lies beside the East-West Highway near Sukhad bazaar in Kailali, about 58 km east of Dhangadhi, 1.5 hours by road. From Bardia's Thakurdwara it is about 110 km and 2.5–3 hours west, so it sits naturally on the drive from Bardia to Shuklaphanta.
The nearest airport is Dhangadhi, about 1 hour 15 minutes by air from Kathmandu. From the airport a private car reaches the lakes in about 1.5 hours via Attariya and the highway.

where_to_stay: Most travellers visit Ghodaghodi as a stop of two or three hours and stay elsewhere: in Bardia to the east, or in Dhangadhi, Attariya or Mahendranagar to the west, which have mid-range hotels. Sukhad bazaar, the market town next to the lakes, has a few simple lodges used by Nepali travellers, with basic rooms and dal bhat. If you want a dawn birding session, a night in Sukhad or Attariya is the practical choice.
tips: Stop in the morning or late afternoon; midday heat sends birds and crocodiles into cover.
Carry binoculars, since most crocodiles and waterbirds are on the far shores.
Keep well back from the water's edge; mugger crocodiles are wild and can be anywhere in the reeds.
Wear long trousers and use mosquito repellent, especially from April onwards.
Ask at the community forest office near the lakes about local guides and any visitor fee; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Birding walk around the main lake
experiences.summary: Walk the forest path along the main lake at dawn with binoculars and a local guide, watching wintering ducks, herons, cormorants, jacanas and kingfishers on one of the Terai's richest wetlands. Easy, flat and close to the road.
body: In the first light the lake is still and grey, and the sounds come first: the honk of ducks, the whistle of a kingfisher, the clatter of a purple swamphen in the reeds. The path from the highway leads into sal forest and along the shore, with gaps in the trees where you can stand and scan the water. Within a few minutes of leaving the highway, the traffic noise fades behind the trees. The light is soft, the air cool, and the birds are at their most active.

In winter the open water holds rafts of ducks and grebes, while egrets, herons and cormorants fish the edges and bronze-winged jacanas walk on the floating leaves. The forest behind holds woodpeckers, barbets, drongos and, with luck, a hornbill. Raptors circle over the lake as the day warms. Look for Eurasian otters slipping along the reed edges early in the morning. Raptors such as fish eagles sometimes perch in tall trees overlooking the water, watching for prey.

A local guide from the community forest group knows the paths and the best viewpoints. Allow two to three hours at a slow pace and finish with tea in Sukhad bazaar before continuing on the highway. The walk is flat and suitable for most ages. Bring binoculars, a bird app or field guide and a light jacket for the early start. Wear shoes that can cope with mud, especially after rain.

faqs.q: Is Ghodaghodi Tal good for birdwatching?
faqs.a: Yes, especially from November to March, when wintering ducks and waterbirds join resident herons, kingfishers, jacanas and forest birds. It was declared a bird sanctuary in 2022. It is not as famous as Koshi Tappu in the east, but for travellers in the far west it is the best wetland stop.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide at Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: It is not strictly required for a walk near the highway, but a local guide helps you find the paths, viewpoints and birds, and keeps you safe near crocodile water. Ask at the community forest office or arrange one through your hotel or agency in advance.

faqs.q: How long does the lake walk take?
faqs.a: Two to three hours covers a good section of the main lake shore at birding pace. Keen birders can spend a full morning exploring the smaller lakes. The ground is mostly flat forest path, muddy in places after rain. Allow extra time if you stop often.

experiences.title: Spotting mugger crocodiles on the far banks
experiences.best_time: Late morning on sunny days, Nov–Feb
experiences.summary: On sunny winter days the mugger crocodiles of Ghodaghodi haul out to bask on the banks. Scan the far shores with binoculars from safe viewpoints along the forest path and count how many you can find.
body: The mugger is the broad-snouted marsh crocodile of South Asia, found in lakes, ponds and slow rivers. A 2021 survey counted 26 across 18 lakes in the Ghodaghodi area, a healthy number for a small wetland next to a highway. Muggers can grow to well over three metres, though most are smaller. They eat fish, birds and small mammals, and they can move overland between nearby lakes and ponds, which helps them survive in a patchwork of wetlands like this one.

Winter is the best season to see them, because they need the sun to warm up after cold nights. From late morning on clear days they lie on mud banks and fallen logs with mouths open, motionless for hours. Scan the far shores slowly; a crocodile looks like a log until it shifts. Look for the ridged back and the broad snout, and for the drag marks they leave as they slide into the water.

Stay on the path and the viewpoints, keep children close and never go down to the water's edge. Muggers are generally wary of people but can be dangerous at close range. Your guide will know which banks they favour this season. Binoculars make all the difference, as most crocodiles are on the far side of the water. Combine the crocodile watch with the birding walk for a full morning at the lakes.

faqs.q: Are the crocodiles at Ghodaghodi dangerous?
faqs.a: They can be if you go close to the water. Mugger crocodiles usually avoid people, but they are large predators. Stay on the forest path and viewpoints, keep children within reach, and never wade, swim or wash at the lake edge. With sensible distance, watching them is safe.

faqs.q: When is the best time to see crocodiles at Ghodaghodi?
faqs.a: Sunny days from November to February, from late morning to mid-afternoon, when they bask to warm up. In hot months they spend more time in the water and are harder to see. After heavy rain the banks are flooded and sightings drop.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a mugger and a gharial?
faqs.a: The mugger has a broad, heavy snout and lives in lakes, marshes and slow rivers. The gharial has a very long, thin snout for catching fish and lives in fast, deep rivers like the Karnali. Ghodaghodi has muggers; for gharial, look on the Karnali in Bardia.

experiences.title: Evening lamps at the lakeside temple
experiences.summary: Visit the small temple near the main lake in the evening, when local families come to offer flowers and light oil lamps, and watch the light fade over the water and forest. A gentle end to a day on the road.
body: The temple at Ghodaghodi is small and simple, set near the shore of the main lake under big trees. It draws people from the surrounding Tharu and hill villages, and from travellers on the highway who stop for a quick prayer before a long drive. Bells hang at the entrance, and the courtyard is shaded and calm. Women bring flowers and rice on small brass plates, and children play under the trees while their parents pray.

At dusk the lamps are lit, a few bells ring and families gather with flowers and rice. It is not a formal ceremony and there is no fixed timetable; you simply watch village worship as it has been done here for generations, with the sounds of birds settling over the lake. The quiet of the lake at this hour, with birds flying to roost, makes it a peaceful place to sit for a while.

On festival days, especially during Dashain and Tihar in autumn and at Maghi in January, the temple is busy and the area fills with stalls. Remove your shoes before the shrine, walk around it clockwise and ask before photographing people at prayer. A small donation in the box is welcome. On festival evenings, stalls sell sweets, bangles and toys, and the atmosphere is cheerful and crowded.

faqs.q: Can foreigners enter the temple at Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: Visitors are generally welcome in the temple area. Remove your shoes, avoid leather near the shrine if asked, walk clockwise and keep your voice low. Some inner shrines in Nepal are open to Hindus only, so follow any sign or the advice of local people.

faqs.q: When is the temple busiest?
faqs.a: Festival days such as Dashain and Tihar in October or November and Maghi in mid-January, plus Saturdays, when local families have their day off. Evenings are always livelier than mornings. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to visit Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: There is usually no fee for the temple itself. The community forest group may charge a small entry or guide fee for walks around the lakes, which supports conservation work. Rules change, so check current status before you travel. Any guide fee is usually small.

experiences.title: Cycling the Tharu villages around the lakes
experiences.summary: Ride a bicycle along village lanes and field paths around Ghodaghodi, past Tharu homesteads, fish ponds and rice fields, with a local guide who can introduce you to families and explain how the lakes feed the villages.
body: The land around the lakes is flat, and village lanes connect Tharu hamlets set among rice fields, mustard and wheat. Cycling is the easiest way to see them: you move slowly enough to stop and talk, and fast enough to cover several villages in an afternoon. The roads are mostly flat dirt lanes, shaded by mango and other trees, with irrigation channels running beside them. Children wave, dogs bark and buffalo carts trundle slowly past.

Tharu houses here are long and low, with clay walls, thatched or tin roofs, and grain stores inside. You will see fish traps of split bamboo drying by doorways, buffalo returning from the fields and, in winter, the yellow of mustard in flower. Many families fish in the lakes and canals and grow rice in fields watered by the wetland. Your guide can explain how the lakes and canals feed the fields.

Bicycles can be hired through local contacts in Sukhad; ask your guide or hotel to arrange one in advance, as there is no formal rental shop for tourists. Finish back at the lakeshore for sunset. Carry water and a torch if you plan to ride back after dark. Wear a hat and sunscreen, as there is little shade in the open fields. Ask your guide before stopping to photograph people or homes.

faqs.q: Can I hire a bicycle at Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: There are no tourist rental shops, but local guides and hotels in Sukhad can usually borrow or hire bicycles from villagers with some notice. Quality varies, so check the brakes before you leave. We arrange bikes when we include the ride in a trip.

faqs.q: Is cycling around Ghodaghodi safe?
faqs.a: On village lanes, yes. Avoid riding on the East-West Highway itself, which has fast buses and trucks. Ride in daylight, keep to the edge of narrow lanes, and give way to buffalo and tractors. A local guide knows the quiet routes.

faqs.q: What will I see on a Tharu village ride?
faqs.a: Clay-walled Tharu homes, rice and mustard fields, fish ponds, grain stores and daily village life, with chances to meet families and see fishing gear and handicrafts. In winter the fields are green and gold, and the light over the lakes at sunset is lovely.

faqs.q: Where is Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: It is in Ghodaghodi municipality in Kailali district, Sudurpashchim Province, beside the East-West Highway near Sukhad bazaar. It is about 58 km east of Dhangadhi and about 110 km west of Bardia's Thakurdwara, so it sits on the main road across the far western Terai.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: Two to three hours is enough for a walk along the main lake, birding and a temple visit. Serious birders may want a full morning or a night nearby for a dawn start. Most travellers visit it as a stop on the drive between Bardia and Shuklaphanta.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: November to March. The weather is cool, winter waterbirds are on the lakes and crocodiles bask on sunny days. April and May are hot, and the monsoon from mid-June to September floods the paths and brings leeches and mosquitoes. Early morning is best for birds.

faqs.q: Why is Ghodaghodi Tal a Ramsar site?
faqs.a: It was listed in 2003 because it is a large, connected system of forest lakes and marshes that supports rare species, including mugger crocodiles, otters and the red-crowned roofed turtle, along with large numbers of waterbirds, and links wildlife habitat between the Siwalik hills and the plains.

faqs.q: Can I swim or boat in Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: No. Swimming is unsafe because of crocodiles, and the lakes are a protected wetland and bird sanctuary. We are not aware of any regular tourist boating. Enjoy the lakes from the forest paths and viewpoints instead. Boating would disturb the birds and crocodiles that make the lakes special.

faqs.q: Is there accommodation at Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: Sukhad bazaar next to the lakes has a few simple lodges for Nepali travellers. For more comfort, stay in Bardia, Attariya, Dhangadhi or Mahendranagar and visit as a stop on the road. Book ahead in the festival season of October and November.

faqs.q: What does Ghodaghodi mean?
faqs.a: In Nepali, ghoda means horse and ghodi mare, so the name reads as horse and mare. Local people give different explanations for the name, and we have not found a reliable written source for any of them, so ask your guide which version their village tells.

faqs.q: Is Ghodaghodi Tal worth a stop?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are driving between Bardia and Shuklaphanta anyway. It breaks a long day with a quiet forest walk, good birds and crocodiles, at almost no extra cost in time. It is not worth a special trip from Kathmandu on its own.

faqs.q: Are there tigers at Ghodaghodi Tal?
faqs.a: Tigers have been recorded in the forests around Ghodaghodi, which form part of a wildlife corridor between the Siwalik hills and the plains. Sightings by visitors are very rare. The lakes are about birds, crocodiles and quiet forest, not big cats.
